title: AWS WAF adds pre-parse text transformations and new text transformations
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with AWS WAF adds pre-parse text transformations and new text transformations
body_text: Today, AWS WAF adds pre-parse text transformations for query arguments and ten new text transformations for use in any rule statement. Both help you normalize request content so that AWS WAF inspects requests the same way your application interprets them. Pre-parse text transformations normalize a raw query string before AWS WAF parses it into key-value pairs, closing HTTP parameter pollution and parser differential evasion gaps. You can chain up to ten transformations, including URL decode, Combine Duplicate Query Arguments by Comma, and Replace Semicolons with Ampersands, then layer standard post-parse transformations on top within a single rule statement. The new text transformations give you more ways to normalize content before inspection, including industry-standard options such as Uppercase, Trim, Remove Whitespace, and SHA256, plus operating-system-aware command line and JavaScript decoding functions developed by the Amazon Threat Research Team. Each new transformation consumes 10 WCUs, with no additional charge beyond standard AWS WAF pricing, and is available in all AWS Regions. To get started, see the following resources: Pre-parse text transformations in AWS WAF: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-preparse-transformation.html Text transformations in AWS WAF: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-transformation.html Getting started with AWS WAF: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/getting-started.html

title: How to Read Thermal Camera Specifications NETD, Resolution, Range & Spectral Band
summary: NETD, resolution, range, and spectral band explained: how to evaluate thermal camera specifications before you buy.
body_text: Reading a thermal imaging system datasheet comes down to understanding a handful of numbers and knowing what each one means for your mission. NETD tells you how sensitive the camera is, resolution tells you how much detail you get, and spectral band tells you what the camera is tuned to see. Range specs (detection, recognition, identification) describe distance under ideal conditions, so treat them as a ceiling, not a promise. Frame rate affects both smooth motion and export compliance, which can reshape your procurement timeline. The best number on paper rarely wins. The spec that matches your operating environment does. Match every spec to how and where the system will actually be used, then hold each vendor to the same short list. A thermal camera datasheet can look like a wall of acronyms and unit symbols. Once you know what each spec is really telling you, the page turns into a straightforward shopping list. For anyone specifying a full thermal imaging system, the goal is to connect a few key numbers to the job the camera has to do, then find premium infrared imaging solutions that fit. Demand for these systems keeps climbing, especially in defense and security, where the U.S. Department of Defense allocated over $3.4 billion to infrared sensor programs in a single budget year. More programs than ever are writing specs, comparing datasheets, and trying to separate marketing numbers from mission fit. This guide walks through the thermal camera specifications that decide that fit: NETD, resolution, range, spectral band, and frame rate. How Do You Read Thermal Camera Specifications? Every thermal imaging system datasheet is built around a few core categories. Get comfortable with these, and you can evaluate almost any complete thermal imaging solution on the market. Here's the quick version of what each number is answering. Spec Plain-English question it answers NETD How faint a temperature difference can it see? Resolution How much detail, and how far? Spectral band What is it tuned to detect? Range (DRI) How far can it detect, recognize, or identify a target? Frame rate How smoothly does it capture motion? The trap most buyers fall into is chasing the best number in every row. A better approach is to decide what your mission actually needs in each category, then spec to those marks without paying for capabilities you'll never use. That mindset turns a page of thermal camera specifications into a set of decisions you can defend. NETD: How Sensitive Is the Camera? NETD stands for Noise Equivalent Temperature Difference, and it's the most useful sensitivity number on the page. In plain terms, it tells you the smallest temperature difference the camera can pick out from background noise. It's measured in millikelvin (mK), and lower is better. A low NETD thermal camera produces a cleaner image and more easily separates a warm target from a similar-temperature background. If your targets barely stand out from their surroundings, such as a person in mild weather or a subtle hot spot, sensitivity does the heavy lifting. If your targets run dramatically hotter or colder than the scene, you can often accept a higher number and spend your budget elsewhere. When you compare a NETD thermal camera spec across vendors, confirm they're quoting it under similar test conditions because the value shifts with the scene and the optics. Thermal Camera Resolution: How Much Detail Do You Get? Resolution is the pixel count of the detector, written as something like 320x240 or 640x480. More pixels mean more detail, and more detail generally means you can pick out smaller targets or see the same target from farther away. It's the spec buyers intuitively understand, which is why it tends to get over-weighted. Higher thermal camera resolution isn't automatically the right call. More pixels can mean a bigger, heavier, more power-hungry system at a higher price, and on some platforms, they push you into stricter export categories. A wide-area scanning role might be better served by a lower-resolution sensor with a wider field of view. The right thermal camera resolution resolves your smallest target at your typical working distance, and no more. This breakdown of resolution across different use cases shows how the tradeoff plays out. Range: Detection, Recognition, and Identification Range is where datasheets get slippery. Most quote three distances based on a long-standing standard, usually shortened to DRI. It helps to know what each really means before you compare them because the words don't mean what most people assume. Detection means you can tell something is there, a heat blob against the background, without knowing what it is. Recognition means you can tell what class it is: person, vehicle, or animal. Identification means you can make out specific features, like which type of vehicle or what a person is carrying. Two things are worth remembering. First, these distances assume near-ideal conditions, so treat any published range as a best case that shrinks in fog, smoke, or heavy humidity. Second, range depends on the lens and field of view as much as the sensor. A longer focal length reaches farther but narrows what you see, so a longer-range thermal imaging system often trades away situational awareness. Decide which distance defines mission success, then spec to that one. Thermal Imaging Spectral Band: What the Camera Is Tuned to See The thermal imaging spectral band tells you which slice of the infrared spectrum the camera detects. Three bands show up most often on datasheets. Band Wavelength Best suited for LWIR (long-wave) 8–14 µm Ambient-temperature targets, people, vehicles, most surveillance and industrial monitoring MWIR (mid-wave) 3–5 µm High-temperature targets and long-range detection, often in cooled systems Broadband (BBIR) 2–14 µm Mixed scenes where hot and subtle targets appear together Most surveillance, security, and industrial monitoring programs land on long-wave infrared because it sees ambient-temperature objects well and works with lower-cost uncooled detectors . Programs that need very hot targets or extreme distances often move to mid-wave infrared , which pairs with cooled detectors for higher sensitivity. If your scene mixes hot and near-ambient targets, a broadband thermal imaging spectral band adds flexibility that a single-band system can't. Matching the band to your targets matters more than almost any other line on the datasheet. Thermal Camera Frame Rate (and Why It Affects Compliance) Frame rate, measured in hertz (Hz), is how many images the system captures each second. A higher thermal camera frame rate produces smoother video, which matters when you're tracking fast movement or imaging from a moving platform. Standard systems run around 30 to 60 Hz, which is plenty for most monitoring and surveillance work. When events happen in milliseconds, you move into high-speed thermal imaging territory, which is a different class of system. Frame rate is also a compliance specification. U.S. export-control rules place license requirements on certain thermal cameras based on frame rate thresholds. If your program might ship internationally, the thermal camera frame rate you spec can affect where you're allowed to sell. Answer that at the specification stage, not at delivery, where a late discovery compresses your schedule. Where Datasheet Numbers Meet Reality A datasheet describes performance under controlled test conditions, and the field is messier. Measured temperature accuracy, for example, depends heavily on a target's surface emissivity. Research on infrared emissivity shows readings can drift as a surface oxidizes over time, so a camera that nails accuracy on a lab reference can read differently on shiny metal. The same caution applies to detection. Thermal imaging sees through fog, smoke, dust, and darkness far better than a visible camera, but it isn't magic. Heavy rain and high-radiance sources like direct sun degrade performance, and range estimates assume cooperative conditions. Read every number as "up to," and confirm real-world performance against your actual operating environment before you commit. 5 Questions to Ask Before You Trust a Thermal Imaging System Datasheet Once you understand the specs, evaluating vendors gets much easier. Run every datasheet through these five questions: What conditions were these numbers measured under? NETD, range, and accuracy all shift with the test setup. Compare thermal imaging system specs that were measured the same way. Does the resolution resolve my smallest target at my working distance? Not the demo distance in a vendor video. Yours. Is the spectral band matched to my targets? Ambient-temperature targets favor LWIR; very hot or long-range targets often favor MWIR. Does the frame rate create a compliance issue? Check export thresholds before you lock the architecture, not after. Who stands behind the system? A partner who engineers and supports the full system is worth more than a slightly better number on a catalog part. Getting clear answers to those five questions turns a page of thermal imaging system specs into a confident buying decision, and it exposes the vendors who can't back their numbers up. Frequently Asked Questions What is the most important spec on a thermal camera datasheet? There isn't a single one. The most important spec is whichever maps to your mission. For faint targets, NETD (sensitivity) leads. For identifying targets at a distance, resolution and range matter most. For the right kind of target, the spectral band decides everything. Read thermal camera specifications as a set, not a ranking. Is a lower or higher NETD better? Lower is better. NETD measures the smallest temperature difference a NETD thermal camera can detect, so a lower millikelvin value means a cleaner, more sensitive image. Just confirm that vendors quote it under comparable conditions. What thermal camera resolution do I need? Enough to resolve your smallest target at your real working distance. Common formats are 320x240 and 640x480, and higher resolutions help with identification at range, but they add cost, size, and sometimes export complexity. Match resolution to the task. LWIR or MWIR: which spectral band should I choose? LWIR (8–14 µm) suits most ambient-temperature surveillance and industrial monitoring and works with affordable uncooled detectors. MWIR (3–5 µm) suits high-temperature targets and long-range detection, usually with cooled detectors. Your targets and environment decide the right thermal imaging spectral band. Turn Specs Into the Right System The best thermal camera specifications on paper and the best ones for your program are rarely the same camera. Once you can read a datasheet for what it really says, you can spec with confidence and hold every vendor to the same standard. Treat specs as the start of a conversation about mission fit, not the end of one. title: Casella Rings in 50 Years at Nasdaq
summary: On Tuesday, June 17, Casella Chairman and CEO John Casella, President Ned Coletta, and Founder and Vice Chairman Doug Casella rang the Opening Bell at the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square in recognition of our 50th Anniversary.
body_text: Casella Rings in 50 Years at Nasdaq Photography courtesy of Nasdaq, Inc. On Tuesday, June 17, Casella Chairman and CEO John Casella, President Ned Coletta, and Founder and Vice Chairman Doug Casella rang the Opening Bell at the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square in recognition of our 50th Anniversary. The day also marked Global Garbageman Day and the official start to National Waste and Recycling Workers Week, and was specifically chosen to recognize the hard work and dedication of the more than 5,000 Casella employees throughout our company. “It’s an honor to be invited to ring the Opening Bell at Nasdaq in recognition of our 50th Anniversary,” said John W. Casella. “Since our initial public offering in 1997, to where we stand today, Nasdaq has been a tremendous partner in our success.” Founded in 1975 as a single truck collection service, Casella has grown its operations to provide solid waste collection and disposal, transfer, recycling, and organics services to more than one million residential, commercial, municipal, institutional, and industrial customers in ten eastern states and provides professional resource management services to over 10,000 customer locations in more than 40 states nationwide. The company’s commitment to being a sustainable enterprise began almost immediately when it established Vermont’s first recycling facility in 1977. As the only waste and recycling company among the founding members of the EPA Climate Leaders program, Casella’s climate leadership has been recognized by the EPA, the Association of Climate Change Officers, the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, and the Climate Registry with a Climate Leadership Award for Excellence in Greenhouse Gas management. According to its most recent Sustainability Report, for every ton of greenhouse gas the company emits through its operations, Casella’s services prevent an estimated 5.6 tons of greenhouse gas emissions elsewhere in the economy. “Sustainable materials management has been the foundation of our business since it began,” said Casella. “We continue to make progress towards a more sustainable future and achieve greater circularity for customers and communities due to the consistent dedication and hard work of more than 5,000 Casella employees. Recognizing all of them on the world stage, on Global Garbageman Day and as a kickoff to Waste and Recycling Workers’ Week, helps to shine a light on all their contributions to society day in and day out.” Global Garbageman Day is a day dedicated to recognizing and celebrating the efforts of the men and women who keep our communities clean by collecting garbage, recyclables, and other waste. This day also acknowledges the broader role of waste management in protecting the environment and making the world a better place, officially marking the beginning of National Waste and Recycling Workers’ Week, a week-long celebration honoring the individuals in the waste and recycling industry for their hard work and dedication. The full Nasdaq Opening Bell ceremony is available to view at casella.com/bell-ringing . Topics: Awards Our People

The news comes just days after Vizcaíno announced, on July 3, his resignation as president of Cádiz CF, a move that has had a […]
body_text: Manuel Vizcaíno steps down from Nomadar’s board of directors by Press | Jul 8, 2026 | News | 0 comments Nomadar Corp. (Nasdaq: NOMA) has confirmed the departure of Manuel Vizcaíno , former president of Cádiz Club de Fútbol, from his roles as co-chairman and member of the company’s board of directors. The news comes just days after Vizcaíno announced, on July 3, his resignation as president of Cádiz CF, a move that has had a direct effect on his position within Nomadar. It was on July 6, 2026 , that the Nasdaq-listed company publicly filed the corresponding material event notifying Vizcaíno’s resignation as director and co-chairman, while simultaneously announcing the appointment of Joaquín Martín as a new member of the board of directors. Martín is not a new face within the organization: since December 2025 he has held the position of CEO Americas and Global Vice Chairman of Nomadar, and previously, since August 2023, served as Chief Communications and Investor Relations Officer , a role he held practically since the company’s founding stage. Over the past three years, the company has been building out the various verticals that make up its global sports platform, a growth process that led to its Nasdaq debut in October 2025 and, more recently, its inclusion in the Russell Microcap Index in the United States.
